entries.title: The ezafe
entries.summary: Put -e between a noun and the word that describes or owns it: kitāb-e man, my book.

blocks.heading: What it does
blocks.body: Dari links two words that belong together with a short -e sound. It joins a noun to the adjective that describes it, or to the person or thing that owns it. English puts the describing word first (a new book). Dari puts the noun first and links the rest to it: kitāb-e naw, literally 'book-of new'.

blocks.heading: You hear it, you don't see it
blocks.body: The -e is usually not written in Dari script. کتاب من is read kitāb-e man, even though nothing between the two words shows it. The transliteration line always shows it, so use that line to learn where it goes.
After -ā, -ō or -ū the ezafe is written as ی: هوای کابل. After -a, and after -ī, it is usually left unwritten, just like after a consonant: خانه ما.

blocks.heading: Chains
blocks.body: You can keep linking: noun, then adjective, then owner, each joined with -e. The last word of the chain takes nothing.

items.en: The weather in Kabul is cold.

blocks.why: The owner comes after the thing, never before it. man kitāb sounds like 'I, book'.
Adjectives follow the noun in Dari. Put the noun first and link the adjective with -e.

blocks.heading: A shorter way to say 'my'
blocks.body: For 'my', 'your' and 'his' or 'her' you will often see an ending on the noun instead of a separate word: کتابم, kitābam, my book. Both are correct. See Possessive endings.

entries.title: Present tense with mē-
entries.summary: mē- + present stem + ending: mēkhānam, I read. One pattern for almost every verb.

blocks.heading: One tense, two English meanings
blocks.body: Dari uses one present tense where English uses two. من نان می‌خورم means both 'I eat bread' and 'I am eating bread'. The rest of the sentence tells you which.

blocks.heading: Learn the stem with the verb

blocks.body: The present stem often looks different from the infinitive, so there is no safe way to guess it. Learn it together with the verb.

items.target: من هر روز به مکتب می‌روم
items.translit: man har rōz ba maktab mērawam
items.en: I go to school every day.

blocks.heading: Saying 'don't'
blocks.body: Change mē- to namē-. Everything else stays the same.

blocks.why: dāshtan, 'to have', takes no mē- in the present. The same goes for 'to be': hastam, never mēhastam.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Kabul speech shortens the most common verbs: mērawam becomes mērum. man becomes ma, and ba before a place is often left out. You will see this spelling in messages and on social media.

entries.title: The object marker rā
entries.summary: Put rā after a specific object: kitāb rā mēkhānam, I read the book.

blocks.heading: What rā marks
blocks.body: rā comes right after the object of the verb when that object is specific: a thing you both have in mind, a named person, or something with 'this' or 'my'. It is how Dari tells 'I read the book' from 'I read books'.

blocks.heading: When to use it
rows: with this or that: īn khāna

blocks.body: With 'me' and 'you', rā joins the pronoun in writing: man + rā is مرا, marā, and tu + rā is ترا, turā.

blocks.heading: After the whole phrase
blocks.body: rā goes after the complete object, however long it is. It never breaks into an ezafe chain.

blocks.why: barādar-e man is one object, so rā waits until the end of it.

blocks.heading: Not for the subject
blocks.body: rā only ever marks the object. The person doing the action never takes it, and a place you go to takes ba, not rā.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In speech and in casual writing rā is usually ra, spelled ره.

entries.title: Pronouns and 'to be'
entries.summary: Six pronouns, each with its own form of 'to be' at the end of the sentence: man shāgird hastam, I am a student.

blocks.heading: Six pronouns
blocks.body: Dari has six personal pronouns. ō means both 'he' and 'she': Dari has no grammatical gender, so adjectives and verbs never change for male or female.

blocks.heading: Polite 'you'
blocks.body: Use shumā with anyone older than you, with strangers and with anyone you want to show respect to, even when you speak to one person. tu is for close friends, children and people your own age you know well.

blocks.why: 'To be' closes the sentence. The word that describes you comes before it.
The form of 'to be' has to match the person. ast is for one person or thing that is not 'I' or 'you': ō, īn (this), kitāb (the book).

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In Kabul, man is said ma and hastam is said astum. People type it this way in messages too.

entries.title: Word order: the verb goes last
entries.summary: Who does it comes first, the verb comes last, and everything else goes in between.

blocks.heading: The basic order
blocks.body: A Dari sentence starts with who does something and ends with the verb. Time, place and the object all go in between.

items.target: من امروز در خانه نان می‌خورم
items.translit: man imrōz dar khāna nān mēkhuram
items.en: I am eating at home today.
He is going to Kabul tomorrow.

blocks.heading: Time can come first
blocks.body: Words like dīrōz (yesterday), imrōz (today) and fardā (tomorrow) often open the sentence, even before who. The verb still stays last.

items.en: Yesterday I went to the bazaar.

blocks.heading: You can drop the pronoun
blocks.body: The ending of the verb already says who: raftam can only mean 'I went'. So the pronoun is often left out.

items.en: Yesterday I went to the bazaar.

blocks.heading: Small words and describing words
blocks.body: One thing works like English: prepositions such as dar (in) and ba (to) go before their noun. One thing does not: adjectives follow the noun, joined with the ezafe.

blocks.why: The object goes before the verb, not after it as in English.

entries.title: Plurals: -hā and -ān
entries.summary: Add -hā to make almost any noun plural: kitāb, kitāb-hā. After a number the noun stays singular.

blocks.heading: -hā works for everything
blocks.body: Add -hā to the end of a noun. It works for things, animals and people. In Dari script it is joined with a half-space, so the word stays readable: کتاب‌ها.

blocks.heading: -ān for people
blocks.body: Nouns for people can also take -ān. It sounds more formal and is common in writing, but -hā is always understood.

blocks.heading: After a number, no plural
blocks.body: A number already says how many, so the noun after it stays singular: dū kitāb, literally 'two book'.

blocks.why: After a number the noun never takes -hā.

blocks.heading: Plural with the ezafe
blocks.body: A -hā plural ends in a vowel, so its ezafe is -ye and is written ی: kitāb-hā-ye man, my books. An -ān plural ends in a consonant and takes a plain -e: dōstān-e man, my friends.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In Kabul speech -hā usually loses its h and becomes -ā. You will see it spelled that way in messages.

entries.title: Asking questions
entries.summary: Put the question word where the answer would go and keep the verb last. For yes or no, just let your voice rise.

blocks.heading: Same order as the answer
blocks.body: Dari does not move words around to ask a question. The question word sits exactly where the answer would sit, and the verb stays at the end.
The letters کی spell kī, who. They can also spell kay, when, but in Kabul 'when' is usually said chi waqt.

items.en: How many brothers do you have?

blocks.heading: chīst: what is
blocks.body: 'What is' is squeezed into one word, chīst: nām-e shumā chīst? What is your name?

blocks.heading: Yes or no questions
blocks.body: Keep the sentence exactly as it is and let your voice rise at the end. In writing, add the Dari question mark ؟. Formal Dari can open with āyā, but you rarely need it. Answer with balē (yes) or na (no).

blocks.why: Dari never moves the verb to the front to make a question. Only your voice changes.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Kabul's everyday 'How are you?' to a friend drops hāl and uses astī, the spoken form of hastī.

entries.title: Saying no: na- and nēst
entries.summary: Put na- in front of the verb: mērawam, namērawam. 'To be' has its own negative: nēstam, I am not.

blocks.heading: One prefix
blocks.body: To make almost any verb negative, put na- in front of it. In the present tense mē- becomes namē-.

items.en: He didn't go to school yesterday.

blocks.heading: Answering no
blocks.body: On its own, 'no' is na, نه, and 'yes' is balē, بلی.

blocks.why: na- joins the verb as a prefix. Written as a separate word, نه is an answer, 'no'.
'To be' does not take na-. Use its own negative forms: nēstam, nēst.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In speech the final t of nēst is usually dropped: nēs. Messages often spell it that way.

entries.title: Possessive endings
entries.summary: Instead of kitāb-e man you can add an ending to the noun: kitābam, my book. Both are correct.

blocks.heading: A shorter 'my'
blocks.body: Dari has two ways to say whose something is. The long way links a pronoun with the ezafe: kitāb-e man. The short way adds an ending to the noun: kitābam. They mean the same; the short way is what you hear most in speech.

blocks.heading: After -a
blocks.body: After a noun ending in -a, the ending is written apart with a half-space. The singular endings keep their vowel, the plural ones lose their e: khāna-am, my house, but khāna-mān, our house.

blocks.heading: With an adjective
blocks.body: The ending goes on the last word of the whole phrase. With an adjective, that is the adjective: barādar-e kalānam, my older brother.

blocks.why: The ending waits until the end of the phrase, after the adjective.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: The spelling is the same, but in Kabul the endings are said -it and -ish: kitābit, kitābish.

entries.title: Prepositions: dar, ba, az, bā
entries.summary: Small words that go before a noun: dar kābul (in Kabul), ba maktab (to school), az khāna (from home), bā dōst (with a friend).

blocks.heading: Before the noun
blocks.body: Prepositions work like English ones: they come right before the noun they belong to.

items.en: He is going to the bazaar.

blocks.heading: ba or dar?
blocks.body: ba is for moving towards a place. For being in a place, use dar.

blocks.why: You are not moving, so the place takes dar, not ba.

blocks.heading: Some take the ezafe
blocks.body: A few words that began life as nouns link to their noun with the ezafe: pusht-e khāna, behind the house; zēr-e mēz, under the table. pēsh-e works the same way and usually means 'at someone's place': pēsh-e dāktar, at the doctor's. barā-ye already carries its ezafe.

blocks.why: Prepositions go before the noun. Only the verb moves to the end of the sentence.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In Kabul speech dar becomes da, usually typed ده, and da is also used where writing has ba: ma da maktab mērum, I go to school.

entries.title: 'There is' and 'to have'
entries.summary: hast says something exists: chāy hast, there is tea. dāram says you have it: chāy dāram, I have tea.

blocks.heading: ast or hast?
blocks.body: For 'it' or 'he' and 'she', Dari has two words. ast links a thing to a description: the tea is hot. hast says that something exists: there is tea. The negative of both is nēst. With every other person there is just one set, hastam, hastī and so on, as on the 'to be' page.

items.en: There is no water in the room.

blocks.heading: To have: dāshtan
blocks.body: When dāshtan means 'to have', it takes no mē- in the present: dāram, not mēdāram. Its negative is nadāram. The same goes for dōst dāram, 'I like'.

blocks.why: hast says a thing exists somewhere. It cannot mean 'I have'. For having, use dāram.

entries.title: Simple past
entries.summary: Take the infinitive, drop -an and add the endings: raftan, raftam, I went.

blocks.heading: Built from the infinitive
blocks.body: Every past form starts from the past stem, which is the infinitive without its final -an: raftan → raft, kardan → kard, khurdan → khurd.
ō takes no ending at all: ō raft, he went. And unlike the present, the simple past has no mē-.

items.en: Yesterday I went to the bazaar.

blocks.heading: Didn't
blocks.body: Put na- in front: naraftam, I didn't go.

right.en: Yesterday I went to the bazaar.

blocks.why: A time word like dīrōz does not make the sentence past. The verb itself has to be in the past.
The ending must match the person, and for ō there is no ending.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: The spelling stays the same, but Kabul speech says the ending -am as -um: raftum, kardum.

entries.title: Comparing: -tar and -tarīn
entries.summary: Add -tar for 'more': kalāntar az, bigger than. Add -tarīn for 'most' and put it before the noun: kalāntarīn shahr, the biggest city.

blocks.heading: More: -tar
blocks.body: To say 'bigger' or 'newer', add -tar to the adjective. The thing you compare with comes after az, which here means 'than'. In careful writing it is joined with a half-space, کلان‌تر, but you will often see it written joined, کلانتر.

items.target: کابل از شهر ما کلان‌تر است
items.translit: kābul az shahr-e mā kalāntar ast
items.en: Kabul is bigger than our city.

blocks.heading: Most: -tarīn
blocks.body: Add -tarīn for 'the most'. Unlike ordinary adjectives, it comes before the noun, with no ezafe.

blocks.heading: Than all of them
blocks.body: Everyday Dari also says 'the most' with az hama, 'than all': az hama kalāntar, the biggest of all.

items.target: این خانه از همه کلان‌تر است
items.translit: īn khāna az hama kalāntar ast
items.en: This house is the biggest of all.

blocks.why: -tarīn words go before the noun and take no ezafe. Only -tar and plain adjectives follow the noun.

entries.title: Talking about the future
entries.summary: In everyday Dari the present tense plus a time word is the future: fardā mērawam, I'll go tomorrow. Writing also has khāham raft.

blocks.heading: Everyday: just the present
blocks.body: For plans and predictions, Dari simply uses the present tense. A time word like fardā (tomorrow) makes it future.

blocks.heading: Written: khāham + past stem
blocks.body: News, books and formal speech use a separate future: the present of khāstan without mē-, followed by the bare past stem of the verb.

items.target: او فردا به کابل خواهد رفت
items.translit: ō fardā ba kābul khāhad raft
items.en: He will go to Kabul tomorrow.

blocks.heading: Not, and compounds
blocks.body: Put na- on khāham: nakhāham raft, I will not go. With a compound verb, khāham sits between the two parts: kār khāham kard.

blocks.why: Only khāham changes for the person. The second verb is always the bare past stem, with no ending.
With mē-, khāham means 'I want'. The future uses it bare.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: In Kabul 'tomorrow' is usually sabā, ba before a place is often left out, and the future is simply the present: mērum.

entries.title: Past and present stems
entries.summary: Every verb has two stems. The past stem (raft) builds the past tenses; the present stem (raw) builds the present, commands and 'want to' forms.

blocks.heading: Two stems per verb
blocks.body: A Dari verb is listed by its infinitive, ending in -an: raftan, to go. Every other form is built from one of its two stems, so learning a verb means learning both.

blocks.heading: The past stem is easy
blocks.body: The past stem is always the infinitive without -an: raftan → raft, kardan → kard. No exceptions.

blocks.heading: The present stem must be learned
blocks.body: The present stem often looks different and cannot be guessed. Most verbs in -īdan are the kind exception: drop the whole -īdan. kharīdan → khar, fahmīdan → fahm, pursīdan → purs. Two common ones do not follow it: dīdan → bīn and shunīdan → shunaw.

items.en: I write a letter every day.

blocks.why: The present is built on the present stem, nawīs, not on the past stem. mēnawishtam means 'I used to write'.

entries.title: Commands with bu-
entries.summary: Put bu- on the present stem to tell someone to do something: bukhur, eat! Add -ēd to be polite: lutfan bukhurēd.

blocks.heading: The command form
blocks.body: A command is the prefix bu- plus the present stem, with no ending. It is how you speak to one person you know well. The prefix is written ب and its vowel is not written. In Afghanistan it is usually said bu-: bukhur, bukun, buraw, bubīn. Some speakers say bi-, and before yā it is always bi-: biyā.

blocks.heading: Polite: add -ēd
blocks.body: To one person you respect, or to several people, add -ēd. Starting with lutfan (please) makes it a polite request.

blocks.heading: Don't
blocks.body: For 'don't', na- replaces the bu- prefix: nakhur, don't eat; naraw, don't go.

blocks.heading: Compound verbs
blocks.body: Compound verbs keep the first part and put the command on kardan, usually without bu-: kār kun, work! kumak kunēd, help!

blocks.why: Commands never take mē-. They take bu-.

blocks.heading: Come!
blocks.body: āmadan, to come, has the stem ā. bu- + ā is written بیا and said biyā, come! To be polite: biyāyēd (بیایید).

entries.title: Want, can, must
entries.summary: mēkhāham, mētawānam and bāyad are followed by a second verb with bu-: mēkhāham burawam, I want to go.

blocks.heading: Two verbs, both with an ending
blocks.body: English says 'I want to go' with an infinitive. Dari uses two finished verbs instead: 'I want' + '(that) I go'. The second verb takes bu- (written ب) and a normal ending. This is called the subjunctive.

blocks.heading: bāyad stays the same
blocks.body: bāyad never changes: the same word for every person. Only the second verb shows who.

blocks.heading: Compound verbs
blocks.body: Compound verbs usually drop bu- in this form: kār kunam rather than kār bukunam.

blocks.heading: Not
blocks.body: Put the negative on the first verb: namēkhāham burawam, I don't want to go. With bāyad, nabāyad means 'must not'.

blocks.why: The second verb is never in the present with mē-. It takes bu-.
The English-style infinitive does not work here. Give the second verb its own ending.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Kabul speech shortens mētawānam to mētānum and burawam to burum.

entries.title: Compound verbs: kār kardan
entries.summary: Many Dari verbs are a noun plus a helper verb: kār kardan, to work. Only the helper changes: kār mēkunam, kār nakardam.

blocks.heading: Meaning plus helper
blocks.body: A large share of Dari verbs are built from a noun or adjective and a small helper verb, most often kardan (to do). The first part carries the meaning; the helper carries the tense and the person.

blocks.heading: Only the helper changes
blocks.body: mē-, na- and the ending all go on the helper. The first part stays in front and does not change. Only khāham, in the formal future, can come between them: kār khāham kard.

blocks.heading: kardan or shudan?
blocks.body: kardan means 'to do' something, shudan means 'to become'. The pair often gives an active and a non-active verb: kharāb kardan, to break something; kharāb shudan, to break down. khush shudan means 'to be pleased'.

blocks.why: mē- belongs to the helper verb, not to the noun in front of it.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: suhbat kardan is the more formal word for 'talking'. In everyday Dari people say gap zadan, and it is fine in writing too. Kabul speech then shortens the verb: gap mēzanēm.

entries.title: Past continuous: mēraftam
entries.summary: Put mē- on the simple past for 'used to' or 'was doing': mēraftam, I used to go, or I was going.

blocks.heading: One form, two meanings
blocks.body: Add mē- to a simple past verb. The result covers two English meanings: a habit in the past ('I used to go') and something that was going on at the time ('I was going').

items.en: I used to go to school every day.
We used to live in Kabul.

blocks.heading: Watch the spelling
blocks.body: For 'he' and 'she' this form can look exactly like the present: می‌خورد is both mēkhurad, he eats, and mēkhurd, he used to eat. Only the context and the pronunciation tell them apart.

items.en: He always used to drink tea.

blocks.heading: Not
blocks.body: Put na- in front of mē-, just as in the present: namēraftam, I didn't use to go.

right.en: I used to go to school every day.

blocks.why: 'Every day' in the past is a habit, so the verb needs mē-. Without it, raftam sounds like one finished action, not a habit.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Kabul speech says the ending -um, and messages usually skip the half-space: میرفتم.

entries.title: Present perfect: rafta-am
entries.summary: Past stem + -a, then a short ending: rafta-am, I have gone. For 'he' or 'she' it is rafta ast.

blocks.heading: When to use it
blocks.body: Use it for experiences ('I have been to Kabul') and for results that still matter now ('he has eaten'). It is also often used for things you heard about or worked out rather than saw. That is why the news writes gufta ast, '(he) has said', for what someone said.

blocks.heading: In script
blocks.body: The -a is written ه, and the endings join it with a half-space: رفته‌ام. Only 'he' or 'she' keeps ast as a separate word.

blocks.heading: Not yet
blocks.body: na- goes on the front: narafta-am, I haven't gone. With hanōz (yet) it means 'not yet'.

blocks.why: The perfect is built on the -a form, rafta, not on the simple past raftam.

entries.title: 'A' and 'some': yak and -ē
entries.summary: Say 'a book' with yak kitāb or with the ending -ē: kitābē. Either is enough, but you will also hear both together: yak rōzē, one day.

blocks.heading: Two ways to say 'a'
blocks.body: Dari has no word for 'the': a plain noun is already definite or general. For 'a', put yak (one) before the noun, or add -ē to its end. Either is enough; yak is more usual in speech, and the two also appear together: yak rōzē, one day.

blocks.heading: With an adjective
blocks.body: With an adjective, -ē moves to the end of the phrase: kitāb-e nawē, a new book.

blocks.heading: Someone, something
blocks.body: Some everyday words are built this way: kasē, someone; chīzē, something; jāyē, somewhere.

blocks.why: yak means 'one', so it cannot go with a plural. For 'some books', use chand (a few).

entries.title: Writing: the half-space
entries.summary: Dari joins some word parts with a half-space, a break between letters without a gap: می‌خوانم, کتاب‌ها.

blocks.heading: What it is
blocks.body: Arabic-script letters join to their neighbours. A half-space stops that join without leaving a gap, so a prefix or ending stays visibly separate but still part of the word.

blocks.why: In careful writing mē- is kept apart with a half-space. Written together (میخوانم) is common in quick typing, as below, but not in edited text.
A full space splits one word into two. mē- is a prefix, not a word.

blocks.heading: On a phone
blocks.body: On a computer with the Persian (Standard) layout, Shift+Space types a half-space. On an Android phone, hold the space bar. In quick messages many people skip it and type میخوانم; you will need to read both.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Casual Kabuli messages rarely use the half-space, partly because spoken forms like کتابا and میرم do not need one.

entries.title: The subjunctive: the bu- form
entries.summary: The bu- form is for actions that are not real yet: wanted, possible or planned. shāyad biyāyad, maybe he'll come; raftam tā nān bukharam, I went to buy bread.

blocks.heading: For what is not real yet
blocks.body: You met the bu- form after 'want', 'can' and 'must'. It is called the subjunctive, and those three are only the start. Dari uses it whenever an action is wished for, possible, needed or planned, but has not happened.

blocks.heading: Words that call for it
rows: mumken ast ki, it may be that
mumken ast ki dēr biyāyad, he may come late
tā nān bukharam, to buy bread
bihtar ast ki, it is better to
bihtar ast ki narawī, better not to go
pēsh az ān ki burawam, before I go

items.target: به بازار رفتم تا نان بخرم
items.translit: ba bāzār raftam tā nān bukharam
items.en: I went to the bazaar to buy bread.

blocks.heading: Someone else does it: ki
blocks.body: When the person who wants is not the person who acts, the second verb gets its own person, usually after ki (that): mēkhāham ki tu biyāyī, I want you to come.

blocks.heading: 'To be' and 'to have'
blocks.body: būdan, to be, has its own subjunctive with no bu-: bāsham, bāshī, bāshad, bāshēm, bāshēd, bāshand. dāshtan, to have, has none at all. Writing uses dāshta bāsham; speech just uses the present: shāyad waqt dāram, maybe I have time.

blocks.heading: Not
blocks.body: For 'not', na- takes the place of bu-: narawam, nakhuram. bāsham simply adds na-: nabāsham. A compound verb puts na- on the helper: kār nakunam.

blocks.why: na- replaces bu-. The two do not go on the same verb.
English says 'to buy', but after tā Dari needs a full verb with its own ending. (barā-ye nān kharīdan, 'for buying bread', does use the infinitive, but not after tā.)

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Kabul speech says ma for man and shortens burawam to burum.

entries.title: Linking words: but, because, then
entries.summary: walē or ammā (but) and chun or zērā (because) join two whole sentences: naraftam, chun marīz būdam, I didn't go because I was sick. awwal and ba'd put events in order.

blocks.heading: And, or
blocks.body: wa (and) and yā (or) join words or whole sentences, as in English: nān wa chāy, bread and tea; chāy yā āb, tea or water.

blocks.heading: But: walē, ammā
blocks.body: walē and ammā both mean 'but'. They start the second half of the sentence.

items.target: هوا سرد بود ولی ما بیرون رفتیم
items.translit: hawā sard būd walē mā bērōn raftēm
items.en: It was cold, but we went out.

items.target: او را دیدم اما با او گپ نزدم
items.translit: ō rā dīdam ammā bā ō gap nazadam
items.en: I saw him, but I didn't talk to him.

blocks.heading: Because: chun, zērā
blocks.body: chun and zērā both mean 'because'. zērā is more formal and only starts the second half. chun can also come first, like English 'since'.

items.target: امروز به مکتب نرفتم، چون مریض بودم
items.translit: imrōz ba maktab naraftam, chun marīz būdam
items.en: I didn't go to school today because I was sick.

items.target: چون باران می‌بارید، در خانه ماندیم
items.translit: chun bārān mēbārīd, dar khāna māndēm
items.en: Since it was raining, we stayed at home.
He didn't come, because he had work.

blocks.heading: So: ba hamīn khātir, pas
blocks.body: For 'so' or 'that's why', say ba hamīn khātir (or az hamīn khātir) at the start of the second half. It is the same khātir as ba khātir-e, because of. pas also means 'so', often at the start of a question: pas chi kunēm? So what shall we do?

items.target: مریض بودم، به همین خاطر نرفتم
items.translit: marīz būdam, ba hamīn khātir naraftam
items.en: I was sick, so I didn't go.

blocks.heading: Telling a story in order
blocks.body: awwal (first), ba'd (then) and ba'd az ān (after that) put past events in order. The verbs stay in the simple past.

items.target: اول نان خوردم، بعد به مکتب رفتم
items.translit: awwal nān khurdam, ba'd ba maktab raftam
items.en: First I ate, then I went to school.

items.target: بعد از آن به خانه آمدم
items.translit: ba'd az ān ba khāna āmadam

right.en: Since I was sick, I didn't go.

blocks.why: zērā only starts the second half. To give the reason first, use chun.

right.en: I didn't go because of the rain.

blocks.why: chun needs a whole sentence after it. Before a single noun, 'because of' is ba khātir-e.

entries.title: Every, all, none: har, hama, hēch
entries.summary: har (every) takes a singular noun: har rōz, every day. hama means all or everyone. hēch (no, none) needs a negative verb: hēch kas nayāmad, nobody came.

blocks.heading: Every: har
blocks.body: har means 'every' or 'each'. The noun after it stays singular, and so does the verb: har shāgird kitāb dārad, every student has a book.

blocks.heading: None: hēch + not
blocks.body: hēch means 'no' or 'not any'. Unlike English, the verb is negative as well: hēch kas nayāmad, nobody came.

blocks.why: English allows only one 'no'. Dari needs both: hēch and a negative verb.

blocks.heading: All: hama
blocks.body: hama on its own means 'everyone', with a plural verb. Before a noun or pronoun it takes the ezafe, which after -a is heard but not written: همه ما, hama-ye mā, all of us; hama-ye shāgirdān, all the students.

items.target: همه ما در کابل زندگی می‌کنیم
items.translit: hama-ye mā dar kābul zindagī mēkunēm
items.en: All of us live in Kabul.

blocks.heading: A few, some: chand, ba'zē
blocks.body: chand means 'a few' and takes a singular noun: chand rōz, a few days. ba'zē means 'some' and is often followed by az: ba'zē az shāgirdān, some of the students.

items.en: I stayed in Kabul for a few days.
Some of the students didn't come.

blocks.why: har is followed by a singular noun, just like English 'every day'.

entries.title: Relative clauses: mardē ki
entries.summary: To say 'the man who came', add -ē to the noun and follow it with ki: mardē ki āmad. ki does the work of who, which and that.

blocks.heading: noun + -ē + ki
blocks.body: To describe a noun with a whole sentence, add -ē to the noun, then ki, then the sentence. The -ē looks like the 'a' ending, but here it points to 'the one that'. ki does the work of English who, which and that.

items.target: مردی که آمد، دوست من است
items.translit: mardē ki āmad, dōst-e man ast
items.en: The man who came is my friend.

items.target: کتابی که دیروز خریدم اینجا است
items.translit: kitābē ki dīrōz kharīdam īnjā ast
items.en: The book I bought yesterday is here.

blocks.heading: When the noun is the object
blocks.body: If the noun is the object of the main verb, rā comes right after it, before ki. In speech, ra often comes after the whole clause instead: kitābē ki kharīdī ra khāndum.

items.en: I read the book you bought.

blocks.heading: Prepositions need a pronoun
blocks.body: English can end with a preposition: 'the house we live in'. Dari cannot. Keep the preposition inside the sentence, with ān (it) for a thing or ō for a person. In speech the pronoun is often an ending instead: khāna-yē ki dar-ash zindagī mēkunēm.

items.target: خانه‌ای که در آن زندگی می‌کنیم کلان نیست
items.translit: khāna-yē ki dar ān zindagī mēkunēm kalān nēst
items.en: The house we live in isn't big.

items.target: مردی که با او گپ زدم داکتر است
items.translit: mardē ki bā ō gap zadam dāktar ast
items.en: The man I talked to is a doctor.

blocks.heading: No -ē after 'my'
blocks.body: A name, or a noun with 'my' or 'your', takes no -ē: it is already specific, and the sentence just adds more about it. In writing, this kind of clause is often set off with commas. With an adjective, -ē goes on the adjective: kitāb-e nawē ki kharīdam.

items.target: دوست من، که داکتر است، فردا می‌آید
items.translit: dōst-e man ki dāktar ast fardā mēāyad
items.en: My friend, who is a doctor, is coming tomorrow.

right.target: مردی که آمد، دوست من است
right.translit: mardē ki āmad, dōst-e man ast
right.en: The man who came is my friend.

blocks.why: کی (kī) asks 'who?'. Inside a description, 'who' is که (ki), written with ه.

blocks.heading: That exact one: ān ... ki
blocks.body: To point at one exact thing, put ān (that) before the noun: ān mardē ki dīrōz āmad, that man who came yesterday.

entries.title: If: agar
entries.summary: For a real 'if', use agar with the bu- form: agar biyāyī, ō rā mēbīnī, if you come, you'll see him. The result is an ordinary present or a command.

blocks.heading: A real 'if'
blocks.body: agar introduces something that may happen. The 'if' half usually comes first and takes the bu- form. The result is in the present, or is a command.

items.en: If you come, you'll see him.

items.target: اگر فردا باران ببارد، به بازار نمی‌رویم
items.translit: agar fardā bārān bubārad, ba bāzār namērawēm
items.en: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go to the bazaar.

blocks.heading: agar with the past
blocks.body: agar with the simple past is also common for something that may happen later. English uses the present here; Dari says it as if it had already happened.

items.target: اگر او آمد، به من بگو
items.translit: agar ō āmad, ba man bugō

blocks.heading: agar with the present
blocks.body: When you take something as already true now, agar takes the ordinary present: 'if (as you say) you are going'.

items.target: اگر به بازار می‌روی، نان بخر
items.translit: agar ba bāzār mērawī, nān bukhar
items.en: If you're going to the bazaar, buy bread.

blocks.heading: dāshtan
blocks.body: dāshtan has no bu- form. After agar, speech uses the plain present: agar waqt dārī, biyā. Careful writing uses dāshta bāshī: agar waqt dāshta bāshī.

blocks.heading: If not
blocks.body: Put na- on the verb in the 'if' half: agar narawī, if you don't go; agar nayāmad, if he doesn't come.

right.target: اگر فردا بیایی، من در خانه می‌باشم
right.translit: agar fardā biyāyī, man dar khāna mēbāsham
right.en: If you come tomorrow, I'll be at home.

blocks.why: As in English 'if you come', not 'if you will come': the 'if' half does not take the khāham future.

blocks.heading: Things that are not true
blocks.body: For something that is not true or did not happen, Dari uses the past continuous in both halves: agar mēdānistam, ba tu mēguftam, if I had known, I would have told you. The same form also means 'if I knew, I would tell you'.

entries.title: When, before, after: waqtē ki
entries.summary: waqtē ki (when) and ba'd az ān ki (after) take an ordinary tense, and a 'when' still to come is often in the simple past. pēsh az ān ki (before) always takes the bu- form: pēsh az ān ki burawam, before I go.

blocks.heading: When: waqtē ki
blocks.body: waqtē ki means 'when' and joins two events. Each verb takes the tense it would have on its own: for past events, both are past.

items.target: وقتی که او آمد، من در خانه بودم
items.translit: waqtē ki ō āmad, man dar khāna būdam
items.en: When he came, I was at home.

items.target: وقتی که باران می‌بارد، در خانه می‌مانیم
items.translit: waqtē ki bārān mēbārad, dar khāna mēmānēm
items.en: When it rains, we stay at home.

blocks.heading: A 'when' still to come
blocks.body: For a 'when' that has not happened yet, Dari often uses the simple past, just as agar can.

items.target: وقتی که به خانه آمدی، به من بگو
items.translit: waqtē ki ba khāna āmadī, ba man bugō
items.en: When you get home, tell me.

blocks.heading: Before: pēsh az ān ki
blocks.body: pēsh az ān ki means 'before'. The verb after it is always in the bu- form, even in a story about the past, because at that moment the action had not happened yet. qabl az ān ki means the same.

items.target: پیش از آن که بروم، نان خوردم
items.translit: pēsh az ān ki burawam, nān khurdam

items.target: پیش از آن که بیایی، به من بگو
items.translit: pēsh az ān ki biyāyī, ba man bugō

blocks.heading: After: ba'd az ān ki
blocks.body: ba'd az ān ki means 'after'. For past events it takes the simple past.

items.target: بعد از آن که نان خوردم، به مکتب رفتم
items.translit: ba'd az ān ki nān khurdam, ba maktab raftam
items.en: After I ate, I went to school.

right.target: پیش از آن که بروم، نان خوردم
right.translit: pēsh az ān ki burawam, nān khurdam

blocks.why: English says 'before I went', but after pēsh az ān ki Dari needs the bu- form, whatever the tense of the story.

blocks.heading: Before a noun
blocks.body: With a noun instead of a sentence, drop ān ki: pēsh az nān, before the meal; ba'd az maktab, after school.

entries.title: Reported speech: guft ki
entries.summary: Report what someone said with ki and keep their original tense: ō guft ki mērawad, he said he was going. Only the person changes.

blocks.heading: Keep the tense
blocks.body: English moves the verb back when it reports: 'I am going' becomes 'he said he was going'. Dari does not. It keeps the verb as it was first said and changes only the person.

parts.text: the words, in their original tense

blocks.heading: He said... → you report
rows: guft ki mērawad, he said he was going
guft ki raft, he said he had gone
guft ki marīz ast, he said he was sick
guft ki namētawānad, he said he couldn't

blocks.why: mēraft moves the action into the past: 'he said he used to go'. Keep the tense he used.

blocks.heading: Questions: pursīd
blocks.body: Report a question with pursīd (asked) and ki, again keeping the tense.

items.target: از من پرسید که کجا می‌روم
items.translit: az man pursīd ki kujā mērawam
items.en: He asked me where I was going.

blocks.heading: Commands: the bu- form
blocks.body: When you report a command or a request, the verb takes the bu- form.

items.target: معلم گفت که کتاب را بخوانیم
items.translit: mu'allim guft ki kitāb rā bukhānēm
items.en: The teacher told us to read the book.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Speech often leaves out ki, and Kabul shortens mērawad to mēra.

entries.title: Past perfect: rafta būdam
entries.summary: The -a form of the verb plus būdam (I was) says 'I had done': waqtē ki āmadī, man rafta būdam, when you came, I had gone.

blocks.heading: Before another past
blocks.body: Use it for something already finished at a moment in the past: 'when you came, I had gone'. It is the -a form from the present perfect (rafta) followed by the past of būdan, to be.

blocks.heading: In script
blocks.body: The two words are written apart, with a full space: رفته بودم. Only būdam changes for the person.

items.target: وقتی که آمدی، من رفته بودم
items.translit: waqtē ki āmadī, man rafta būdam
items.en: When you came, I had already gone.

items.target: وقتی که او را دیدم، نان خورده بود
items.translit: waqtē ki ō rā dīdam, nān khurda būd
items.en: When I saw him, he had already eaten.

blocks.heading: Not
blocks.body: na- goes on the first word: narafta būdam, I hadn't gone. A compound verb keeps its first part in front: kār nakarda būdam.

items.target: من پیش از آن کابل را ندیده بودم
items.translit: man pēsh az ān kābul rā nadīda būdam
items.en: I had not seen Kabul before that.

blocks.heading: Have or had?
blocks.body: rafta-am links the past to now: I have gone, and I am still away. rafta būdam links it to a moment in the past: by then, I had gone.

blocks.why: The first word is the -a form, rafta, with no ending. Only būdam shows the person.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Kabul speech says the ending -um here too, so the spelling stays the same. Speech also uses this form for a trip you made and came back from: dīrōz bāzār rafta būdum, I went to the bazaar yesterday (and I'm back).

entries.title: The passive: nawishta shud
entries.summary: For 'it was done', put the -a form of the verb before shudan: nāma nawishta shud, the letter was written. The doer is usually left out.

blocks.heading: Something was done
blocks.body: To say what happened to something without saying who did it, use the -a form of the verb (nawishta, written) with shudan, to become. Literally: 'the letter became written'.

blocks.heading: With nawishtan (to write)
rows: nawishta shuda ast, it has been written
nawishta khāhad shud, it will be written

blocks.heading: Only shudan changes
blocks.body: The -a form stays the same. mē-, na- and the ending go on shudan, just as with kharāb shudan on the compound verbs page. In the bu- form, shudan usually drops bu-: bāyad nawishta shawad, it must be written.

items.target: این کتاب در کابل خوانده می‌شود
items.translit: īn kitāb dar kābul khānda mēshawad
items.en: This book is read in Kabul.
This road has not been built.

blocks.heading: It is said that
blocks.body: gufta mēshawad ki means 'it is said that', and the news uses the passive often. Everyday speech prefers an active verb with 'they': mēgōyand ki, they say that.

items.target: گفته می‌شود که او در کابل است
items.translit: gufta mēshawad ki ō dar kābul ast
items.en: It is said that he is in Kabul.

blocks.heading: Who did it?
blocks.body: If you want to say who did it, an active verb is usually more natural: man nāma rā nawishtam, I wrote the letter.

blocks.why: The passive needs the -a form, nawishta. The bare past stem goes with khāham, in the future.

entries.title: Building words: -ī, -gar, bē-
entries.summary: A few endings and prefixes make new words from ones you know: āzād (free) → āzādī (freedom), kār (work) → kārgar (worker), adab (manners) → bē-adab (rude).

blocks.heading: Guessing new words
blocks.body: Dari builds many words from a small set of endings and prefixes. Once you know them, you can often guess a new word from one you already know.

blocks.heading: -ī: ideas and origins
blocks.body: Added to an adjective or a noun, -ī makes a noun for the idea: āzād, free → āzādī, freedom. Added to a place, it means 'from there': kābul → kābulī.
After -a, the ending becomes -gī and the ه is dropped: زنده → زندگی.

items.target: من زندگی در کابل را دوست دارم
items.translit: man zindagī dar kābul rā dōst dāram

blocks.heading: People, holders and places
blocks.body: -gar makes the person who does something. -dān makes something that holds. -stān makes a place.

blocks.heading: Prefixes: nā-, bē-, bā-
blocks.body: nā- means 'not'. bē- means 'without' and bā- means 'with', so they often make opposite pairs. bē- is usually written with a half-space, بی‌ادب, but some very common words are written joined, like بیکار.

entries.title: If I had known: unreal 'if'
entries.summary: For something that is not true, or did not happen, both halves take the mē- past: agar mēdānistam, namēraftam, if I had known, I wouldn't have gone.

blocks.heading: Real or unreal
blocks.body: An 'if' sentence can be about something that can still happen: agar burawī or agar raftī, if you go. That kind takes the subjunctive, or just as often the simple past. This page is about the other kind: something that is not true now, or that did not happen. For that, Dari puts mē- on the past verb in both halves.

items.en: If I had known, I wouldn't have gone.

items.target: اگر زودتر می‌آمدی، او را می‌دیدی
items.translit: agar zūdtar mēāmadī, ō rā mēdīdī
items.en: If you had come earlier, you would have seen him.

blocks.heading: Now or in the past?
blocks.body: The same form covers both: agar mēdānistam can mean 'if I knew' or 'if I had known'. The rest of the sentence usually makes it clear.

items.target: اگر دری می‌دانستم، با او گپ می‌زدم
items.translit: agar darī mēdānistam, bā ō gap mēzadam
items.en: If I knew Dari, I would talk to him.

blocks.heading: Clearly in the past
blocks.body: To make the 'if' half clearly past, you can use the past perfect instead: agar dīda būdam, if I had seen. The result half keeps the mē- past.

items.target: اگر او را دیده بودم، به او می‌گفتم
items.translit: agar ō rā dīda būdam, ba ō mēguftam
items.en: If I had seen him, I would have told him.

blocks.heading: Not
blocks.body: Put na- in front of mē-, as usual: agar namēāmadī, if you hadn't come. With the past perfect it goes on the front of the first word: agar narafta būdam, if I hadn't gone.

items.target: اگر باران نمی‌بارید، به بازار می‌رفتیم
items.translit: agar bārān namēbārīd, ba bāzār mēraftēm
items.en: If it weren't raining, we would go to the market.

right.en: If I had known, I wouldn't have gone.

blocks.why: The result half needs mē- too. naraftam only says 'I didn't go'. namēraftam says 'I wouldn't have gone'.

wrong.target: اگر زودتر آمدی، او را می‌دیدی
wrong.translit: agar zūdtar āmadī, ō rā mēdīdī

right.target: اگر زودتر می‌آمدی، او را می‌دیدی
right.translit: agar zūdtar mēāmadī, ō rā mēdīdī
right.en: If you had come earlier, you would have seen him.

blocks.why: agar with the simple past is a real 'if': agar āmadī usually means 'if you come'. It can never mean 'if you had come'. For something that did not happen, use the mē- past in both halves.

entries.title: Wishes with kāsh
entries.summary: kāsh means 'if only'. The verb after it says what kind of wish: kāsh mēāmad, if only he would come; kāsh āmada būd, if only he had come; kāsh biyāyad, I hope he comes.

blocks.heading: If only
blocks.body: kāsh means 'if only' or 'I wish'. It does not change. In speech it is often kāshki (کاشکی). The verb after it tells you what kind of wish it is.

blocks.heading: Three kinds of wish
rows: if only he would come, or had come (he didn't)
if only he had come (too late now)
I hope he comes (it can still happen)

blocks.heading: Not true now
blocks.body: For something you want but do not have, use the mē- past, just as in an unreal 'if'.

items.en: I wish I knew Dari better.

blocks.heading: Regrets
blocks.body: For something in the past that you are sorry about, use the past perfect. The mē- past works here too, and in speech it is the more common: kāsh wa'da namēdādam, I wish I hadn't promised.

items.en: If only I had seen him.

blocks.heading: Hopes
blocks.body: When the wish can still come true, use the subjunctive with bu-. It is close to English 'I hope'. For hopes about the weather, health or luck, Dari more often says khudā kunad ki, 'God grant that'.

items.en: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.

items.target: خدا کند که فردا باران نبارد
items.translit: khudā kunad ki fardā bārān nabārad
items.en: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.

blocks.why: The present with mē- does not follow kāsh. Use the mē- past, or the subjunctive for a hope: kāsh biyāyad.

entries.title: May have, must have: rafta bāshad
entries.summary: The -a form plus bāsham, bāshī, bāshad guesses about the past: shāyad rafta bāshad, he may have gone; bāyad rafta bāshad, he must have gone.

blocks.heading: Guessing about the past
blocks.body: When you are not sure something happened, or you work it out from what you can see, Dari uses the perfect subjunctive. It is the -a form of the verb, as in rafta, followed by bāsh- and a normal ending.

blocks.heading: May have: shāyad
blocks.body: shāyad (maybe) with this form says that something may have happened. For 'not', na- goes on the -a form: narafta bāshad.

items.en: Maybe they haven't read the letter.

blocks.heading: Must have: bāyad
blocks.body: bāyad with this form is a confident guess: it must have happened. With the plain subjunctive, bāyad burawad, it is a duty instead: he must go.

items.target: او در خانه نیست، باید به بازار رفته باشد
items.translit: ō dar khāna nēst, bāyad ba bāzār rafta bāshad
items.en: He isn't at home. He must have gone to the market.

items.target: فکر نمی‌کنم که او رفته باشد
items.translit: fikr namēkunam ki ō rafta bāshad
items.en: I don't think he has gone.

blocks.why: After bāyad the helper is bāshad, not ast. After shāyad, bāshad is also the normal choice.

blocks.heading: Should have
blocks.body: 'Should have' is a different form. For something that ought to have happened but did not, use bāyad with the mē- past.

entries.title: Although and even so
entries.summary: agarchi and harchand mean 'although'. bā wujūd-e means 'despite'. bā īn ham, 'even so', starts a sentence that goes against the one before.

blocks.heading: Although
blocks.body: agarchi and harchand both mean 'although' or 'even though'. They open the half of the sentence that you admit is true. The other half says what happened anyway.

items.en: Although I was tired, I worked.

items.target: هرچند باران می‌بارید، به مکتب رفتیم
items.translit: harchand bārān mēbārīd, ba maktab raftēm
items.en: Even though it was raining, we went to school.

blocks.heading: With walē or ammā
blocks.body: English says 'although' or 'but', not both. Dari often starts the second half with walē or ammā (but) as well.

items.target: اگرچه پول نداشت، ولی خوش بود
items.translit: agarchi pūl nadāsht, walē khush būd
items.en: Although he had no money, he was happy.

blocks.heading: Despite
blocks.body: bā wujūd-e means 'despite'. Before a noun that is enough: bā wujūd-e bārān, despite the rain. Before a whole clause, the written form is bā wujūd-e ān ki or bā wujūd-e īn ki. Speech shortens it to bā wujūd-e ki.

items.target: با وجود باران به بازار رفتیم
items.translit: bā wujūd-e bārān ba bāzār raftēm
items.en: Despite the rain, we went to the market.

items.target: با وجود آن که مانده بود، کار کرد
items.translit: bā wujūd-e ān ki mānda būd, kār kard

blocks.heading: Even so
blocks.body: bā īn ham (even so) and bā wujūd-e īn (despite this) start the second of two sentences, when it goes against the first.

items.target: باران می‌بارید، با این هم بیرون رفتیم
items.translit: bārān mēbārīd, bā īn ham bērōn raftēm
items.en: It was raining. Even so, we went out.

blocks.heading: Even if
blocks.body: Put ham (also, even) into the 'if' half and agar becomes 'even if'.

items.en: Even if it rains, I will go.

entries.title: Until, as soon as, while
entries.summary: tā means 'until' with the subjunctive and 'as soon as' with the past. hamīn ki is 'the moment that'. dar hālē ki is 'while'.

blocks.heading: tā: until
blocks.body: tā has several jobs. With the subjunctive it means 'until', for something that has not happened yet. It can also mean 'so that'.

blocks.heading: The extra 'not'
blocks.body: When tā means 'until', Dari usually puts na- on the verb in the tā half, whether or not the main verb is negative. It still means 'until': do not translate that na- as 'not'. Without na-, tā ki with a present or past verb means 'as long as' or 'while'.

items.target: تا کار تمام نشود، به خانه نمی‌روم
items.translit: tā kār tamām nashawad, ba khāna namērawam
items.en: I won't go home until the work is finished.

items.target: تا کار تمام نشود، اینجا باش
items.translit: tā kār tamām nashawad, īnjā bāsh
items.en: Stay here until the work is finished.

blocks.heading: As soon as: tā and hamīn ki
blocks.body: With a past verb, tā means 'as soon as'. hamīn ki means the same, and stresses the very moment: one thing happens and the other follows at once.

items.en: As soon as he saw me, he laughed.

items.target: همین که به خانه رسیدم، باران شروع شد
items.translit: hamīn ki ba khāna rasīdam, bārān shurū' shud
items.en: The moment I got home, it started to rain.

blocks.heading: While: dar hālē ki
blocks.body: dar hālē ki joins two things happening at the same time. It is also used for a contrast, like English 'whereas'.

items.target: در حالی که نان می‌خوردم، او آمد
items.translit: dar hālē ki nān mēkhurdam, ō āmad
items.en: While I was eating, he came.

items.target: او کار می‌کند، در حالی که برادرش درس می‌خواند
items.translit: ō kār mēkunad, dar hālē ki barādarash dars mēkhānad
items.en: He works, whereas his brother studies.

blocks.heading: Which one?
rows: the moment that: one thing right after another
while: two things at once; also 'whereas'

blocks.why: 'Until' points to something that has not happened yet, so the verb after tā takes the subjunctive, not mē-.

entries.title: One can, one must: mētawān guft
entries.summary: mētawān and bāyad with the short infinitive make a sentence about anybody: mētawān guft, one can say; bāyad raft, it's time to go. mēgōyand means 'people say'.

blocks.heading: A sentence about anybody
blocks.body: English often says 'you' or 'one' when it means anybody: 'you can see Kabul from here'. Dari leaves the person out. It uses mētawān (one can) or bāyad (one must) with the short infinitive. This is written Dari. In speech, Kabul says ādam bāyad ... ('a person must ...') or puts mēsha after the -a form: az īnjā kābul dīda mēsha, you can see Kabul from here.

blocks.heading: The short infinitive
blocks.body: Take -an off an infinitive and you have the short infinitive: raftan → raft, guftan → guft, dīdan → dīd. It looks like the past for 'he' or 'she', but here it has no time and no person.

rows: one must go; it's time to go

items.target: از اینجا می‌توان کابل را دید
items.translit: az īnjā mētawān kābul rā dīd
items.en: From here you can see Kabul.

items.target: با این پول موتر نمی‌توان خرید
items.translit: bā īn pūl mōtar namētawān kharīd
items.en: You can't buy a car with this money.

blocks.heading: When you mean a person
blocks.body: For a particular person, use the subjunctive with an ending instead: bāyad burawam, I must go. The short infinitive is for anybody.

blocks.why: After mētawān, and after bāyad used this way, the verb loses its -an. guftan is the full infinitive.

blocks.heading: People say: mēgōyand
blocks.body: For 'people say' or 'it is said', Dari uses mēgōyand, 'they say', without saying who. The news also uses the passive gufta mēshawad, 'it is said'.

items.target: می‌گویند که او به کابل رفته است
items.translit: mēgōyand ki ō ba kābul rafta ast
items.en: They say he has gone to Kabul.

items.target: گفته می‌شود که او مریض است
items.translit: gufta mēshawad ki ō marīz ast
items.en: It is said that he is ill.

blocks.heading: In everyday speech
blocks.note: Kabul speech shortens mēgōyand to mēgan, and people type it میگن.

entries.title: Verbs as nouns: raftan, kōshish
entries.summary: The infinitive also works as a noun: raftan ba kābul āsān nēst, going to Kabul is not easy. Formal writing then links ideas with words like binābar'īn, therefore.

blocks.heading: The infinitive is a noun
blocks.body: raftan means 'to go', but it also works as a noun: 'going'. It can be the subject of a sentence, and it can follow a preposition. English uses -ing for this.

items.en: Going to Kabul is not easy.

blocks.heading: Its object
blocks.body: What you do can follow with the ezafe, khāndan-e kitāb, or come first with no ezafe, kitāb khāndan. For 'reading books' in general both work, and kitāb khāndan is the everyday one. For one particular book, use the ezafe (khāndan-e īn kitāb) or rā (īn kitāb rā khāndan).

blocks.heading: After prepositions
blocks.body: The infinitive is common after barā-ye (for), pēsh az (before) and ba'd az (after).

items.en: Have some tea before you go.

right.en: Have some tea before you go.

blocks.why: pēsh az goes straight onto a noun, and the infinitive is one. A verb with an ending needs pēsh az ān ki and the subjunctive: pēsh az ān ki burawī.

blocks.heading: Nouns in -ish
blocks.body: Many abstract nouns are a present stem plus -ish. You cannot make new ones freely, but once you know the stem they are easy to recognise.

blocks.heading: Linking ideas in writing
blocks.body: Formal writing and speeches organise an argument with a few set phrases. binābar'īn means 'therefore'. az yak taraf ... az taraf-e dīgar means 'on the one hand ... on the other hand'. In everyday talk people say az hamīn khātir (that's why) instead: mānda būdam, az hamīn khātir naraftam.

items.en: I was tired, so I didn't go.

items.target: از یک طرف کار زیاد است، از طرف دیگر وقت کم است
items.translit: az yak taraf kār ziyād ast, az taraf-e dīgar waqt kam ast
items.en: On the one hand there is a lot of work; on the other, there is little time.

entries.title: Written Dari and Kabul speech
entries.summary: Kabul speech shortens written Dari in regular ways: man becomes ma, hastam becomes astum, mērawam becomes mērum. Write the full forms, and learn to read both.

blocks.heading: Two ways to say the same thing
blocks.body: The other pages teach written Dari: the language of books, news and school. In Kabul, people speak a shorter form of it, and they type that form in messages too. Most words stay the same, and the changes follow a few regular patterns.

blocks.heading: Which to use
blocks.body: Write the full forms. If you speak them you will be understood everywhere, though in conversation full forms like mērawam and hastam sound like reading aloud from a book. Learn the Kabul forms so you can follow people and read what they send you.
mā (we) and shumā (you) stay the same in speech.

blocks.note: dar becomes da (typed ده), and hastēm becomes astēm. mā stays mā.

blocks.heading: Verbs
blocks.body: Speech changes some endings: -am is said -um, -ad is said -a, and -ēd becomes -ēn. The commonest verbs also lose part of their stem, so mērawam becomes mērum.

blocks.heading: Small words
blocks.body: rā is said ra and typed ره. After a consonant it is often just -a, joined to the word: kitāba, 'the book' (object). dar becomes da, typed ده, and da also stands where writing has ba. ba before a place is often left out. The plural -hā loses its h: kitābā.

blocks.note: man becomes ma, -hā becomes -ā, rā becomes ra, and the ending -am is said -um. Messages usually skip the half-space too.
chi is said chī and typed چی, and mēgōyad becomes mēga.
